title: THE MIDIANITE WAR ENDED WITH AN ORDER MOST CHRISTIANS WOULD RATHER NOT READ ALOUD
paragraphs: THE MIDIANITE WAR ENDED WITH AN ORDER MOST CHRISTIANS WOULD RATHER NOT READ ALOUD

Numbers 31 contains words about women, children, judgment, and war that can make even a devoted Christian recoil. But perhaps the answer is not to hide the passage—or defend it carelessly. Perhaps we need to stand before the text long enough to discover what it actually says, what it does not say, and why the road from this terrible battlefield ultimately makes us desperate for Jesus Christ.
There are Bible passages we embroider on pillows.
Numbers 31 is not one of them.
There are verses we underline because they comfort us when the night is long. Verses we send to a grieving friend. Verses we whisper over our children before they sleep.
And then there are passages like this.
Passages that make the room uncomfortable.
Passages that make believers lower their voices and skeptics raise theirs.
Passages that do not seem interested in protecting our feelings.
Numbers 31 is one of those passages.
Israel goes to war against Midian.
Men die.
Cities and encampments burn.
Women and children are taken captive.
The soldiers return.
And then Moses discovers that the women have been spared.
His response is terrifying.
He reminds the commanders of what happened at Peor and of the role attributed to Balaam's counsel. Then comes the sentence many readers wish were not in their Bible.
The Hebrew of Numbers 31:17–18 reads in part:
“וְעַתָּה הִרְגוּ כָל־זָכָר בַּטָּף … וְכֹל הַטַּף בַּנָּשִׁים אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יָדְעוּ מִשְׁכַּב זָכָר הַחֲיוּ לָכֶם”
A close rendering is:
“Now therefore kill every male among the little ones … but all the female children who have not known a man’s bed, keep alive for yourselves.”
That is substantially what the Hebrew says.
Read it again.
Slowly.
Do not rush past it because you are afraid of what somebody might ask you.
Do not soften it into something it is not.
But do not make it more horrifying than the text itself says, either.
Because if we love Scripture, we owe Scripture more than defense.
We owe it honesty.
And here is where that honesty becomes crucial.

The Hebrew expression translated “have known a man” refers to sexual experience. The females spared in verse 18 are specifically described as those who had not “known a man’s bed”; translation notes identify them as girls or female children.
But Numbers 31:18 does not say that these girls were preserved for rape.
It does not explicitly say that they were preserved to become sexual slaves.
It does not describe soldiers being given permission to sexually abuse them.
Those conclusions are sometimes inserted into the passage as though the verse explicitly says them.
It does not.
That matters.
But so does this:
The text is still disturbing.
We do Christianity no favors when we pretend otherwise.

Even after removing sensational claims that go beyond the words on the page, we are still looking at warfare, killing, captivity, judgment, terrified survivors, dead children, and a command that collides violently with modern moral instincts.
There is no clever Hebrew word that makes all of that disappear.
There is no theological sentence that turns a battlefield into a greeting card.
There should not be.
The Bible is brutally honest about a world ruined by sin.
And perhaps before asking why Numbers 31 is so violent, we need to remember what happened before Numbers 31.
There was Peor.

Numbers 25 describes Israel being drawn into idolatry and sexual immorality connected with the worship of Baal of Peor. A plague followed. Twenty-four thousand Israelites died according to the narrative.
And the Midianite connection was not incidental.

Numbers 25:16–18 specifically identifies Midianite hostility and deceit in connection with Peor, while Numbers 31:16 looks backward and says that through Balaam's counsel the Israelites were caused to act unfaithfully against the LORD in that affair.
So Numbers 31 is not presented as Israel randomly waking up one morning and deciding to slaughter innocent neighbors for territory.
Within the narrative, it is presented as divine judgment connected to the catastrophe at Peor.
That context matters enormously.
It does not make the deaths emotionally easy.
It tells us what kind of claim the biblical writer is making.
This is judgment.
And that word makes modern people uncomfortable.
Sometimes Christians too.
Because we love hearing that God is merciful.
He is.
We love hearing that God forgives.
He does.
We love hearing that God restores sinners.
He absolutely does.
But the same Bible that says God is merciful refuses to tell us that evil is ultimately inconsequential.
Sin destroys things.
Sin destroys people.
Sin destroys families.
Sin destroys nations.
And sometimes we speak about sin so casually because we have never watched it finish eating somebody alive.
Peor shows us what temptation looks like when the music is still playing.
Numbers 31 shows us a world after the bill arrives.
That is terrifying.
Because we are usually fascinated by the beginning of sin.
Scripture keeps showing us the end.
At the beginning, temptation whispers.
At the end, somebody is crying.
At the beginning, compromise looks manageable.
At the end, generations can be carrying wounds nobody remembers how to explain.
At the beginning, Balaam could not curse Israel.
So according to Numbers 31:16, another avenue became devastatingly effective.
Seduction.
Compromise.
Unfaithfulness.
And perhaps that is where this ancient battlefield suddenly stops feeling so ancient.
Because some of the greatest battles for your soul will not arrive looking like battles.
They will arrive looking attractive.
Convenient.
Private.
Harmless.
Deserved.
Nobody needs to know.
Just once.
You're lonely.
You're angry.
God will forgive you anyway.
And somewhere between the first compromise and the hundredth excuse, something inside you begins dying.
Maybe that is why this chapter bothers us so deeply.
We want sin to be small and grace to be enormous.
Scripture says grace is enormous precisely because sin is not small.
But another question remains.
A harder one.
What about the children?
What about those who died who were not personally responsible for seducing Israel at Peor?
What about collective judgment?
What about the female children who survived and became captives?
Those questions should not be mocked.
They should not be silenced with “just have faith.”
Faith is not pretending a difficult verse is easy.
Christians have wrestled with texts of divine judgment for centuries because Scripture itself gives us a God who is perfectly just while also giving us narratives whose severity can overwhelm us.
Numbers 31 does not provide answers to every moral and emotional question a twenty-first-century reader will bring to it.
We should have the humility to admit that.
There is also something else in the chapter that deserves attention.
After the battle, those who killed or came into contact with the dead could not simply stroll back into Israel's camp celebrating.
They remained outside the camp and underwent purification.
Numbers 31:19 says:
“וְאַתֶּם חֲנוּ מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה שִׁבְעַת יָמִים”
“And you, encamp outside the camp seven days…”
Those who had killed or touched the slain had to undergo purification, and the captives were included in the purification instructions as well.
That detail does not erase the killing.
But it should stop us from reading biblical warfare as though bloodshed were casual entertainment.
Death contaminates.
Death belongs to the brokenness of this world.
Even after a battle the narrative presents as commanded judgment, contact with death requires purification.
The soldiers do not return from killing and immediately walk untouched into sacred space.
There is a boundary.
There is cleansing.
There is death outside.
There is holiness within.
And thousands of years later, another Man would stand outside.
Not carrying a sword.
Carrying a cross.
Jesus.
And suddenly the entire Bible begins pulling our eyes toward something Numbers 31 could never accomplish.
Because Numbers 31 can show judgment.
But Numbers 31 cannot become the final answer to the human problem.
Israel itself would sin again.
And again.
And again.
The people commissioned to execute judgment would themselves need mercy.
Moses needed mercy.
Israel needed mercy.
Midian needed mercy.
You need mercy.
I need mercy.
The scandal of Scripture is not merely that God judges sinners.
The scandal of grace is that God came to save them.
At the cross, God did not announce that sin never mattered.
He demonstrated just how much it mattered.
Christianity does not proclaim a God who simply shrugged at human wickedness and said, “Forget about it.”
The Gospel proclaims Christ crucified.
The Son of God entered our violent, corrupted, rebellious world.
He was betrayed.
Beaten.
Mocked.
Condemned.
Crucified.
And instead of calling His followers to imitate ancient Israel's national warfare, Jesus told His disciples to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them.
The kingdom was moving toward its appointed fulfillment through a crucified Messiah.
This distinction matters desperately.
The church is not ancient Israel camped beside the Jordan.
Christians have no mandate from Numbers 31 to conduct religious warfare against unbelievers.
The enemies Christ commands His followers to love are not targets for a Christian sword.
The Gospel advances through witness, truth, sacrificial love, holiness, proclamation, suffering, prayer, and the power of the Holy Spirit—not forced conversion and not holy war.
Look at Jesus.
When Peter reached for a sword at Christ's arrest, Jesus stopped him.
When Christ stood before Pilate, He declared that His kingdom was not of this world in the manner of earthly kingdoms; otherwise, His servants would fight.
Then the King allowed Himself to be crucified.
Think about that.
The One with the legitimate authority to judge the world chose, at His first coming, to endure judgment for sinners.
The Judge stepped beneath judgment.
The Holy One was treated like the guilty.
The Innocent One was condemned.
The King wore thorns.
The hands that formed humanity were pierced by humanity.
And from the cross came not a warrior's scream for revenge, but words of forgiveness.
That does not mean judgment vanished.
The New Testament still speaks soberly about final judgment.
Jesus did not save us by declaring evil imaginary.
He saves sinners from something real.
And that means Numbers 31 should never make Christians bloodthirsty.
It should make us tremble.
Because if God's judgment against evil is real, then none of us should be standing around congratulating ourselves that we are not Midianites.
The question is not merely:
“What happened to them?”
The question eventually becomes:
“How can any sinner stand before a holy God?”
And Christianity gives an answer so astonishing that we sometimes become numb to it.
Jesus Christ.
Not your religious résumé.
Not the fact that you grew up Christian.
Not the verses in your bio.
Not the worship songs in your playlist.
Not the cross hanging around your neck.
Christ.
Your righteousness cannot save you.
Your excuses cannot save you.
Your secret goodness cannot cancel your secret sin.
But Jesus saves sinners.
This is where the battlefield reaches your bedroom.
Your browser history.
Your private messages.
Your bitterness.
Your addiction.
Your pride.
Your hidden affair.
Your unforgiveness.
Your double life.
Your carefully maintained Christian appearance.
Your secret anger at God.
Your compromise nobody has discovered yet.
You may never stand on the plains of Moab.
But you know Peor.
You know what it is to feel something pulling your heart away from God.
You know what it is to rename disobedience so you can sleep beside it.
And maybe you have been telling yourself:
It isn't that serious.
Numbers 31 whispers something frightening across the centuries:
Sin becomes serious long before we decide to call it serious.
But Calvary says something even louder:
There is mercy for the sinner who comes home.
Not cheap mercy.
Blood-bought mercy.
Not permission to continue hiding.
Grace that drags hidden things into the light and says:
You don't have to die here.
Repent.
Come home.
Christ still receives sinners.
Maybe that is the word somebody reading this needs tonight.
Come home.
Not when you have fixed yourself.
Not after you become worthy.
Not after you have successfully hidden the evidence.
Come to Christ honestly.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Let the Savior meet the person underneath the performance.
Because repentance is not God humiliating you for returning.
Repentance is the road by which the prodigal discovers the Father was worth coming home to.
And grace is not Jesus pretending your scandal never happened.
Grace is Jesus refusing to let your scandal have the final word.
That is why our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior remains:
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because history can be erased.
Not because painful Bible passages become painless.
But because Jesus Christ enters stories filled with rebellion, shame, judgment, wreckage, captivity, and death—and writes redemption where human beings expected only an ending.
If this passage disturbed you, do not run from Scripture.
Dig deeper.
Ask harder questions.
Read context.
Learn the languages when you can.
Refuse sensational interpretations that say more than the text says.
And refuse shallow interpretations that say less than the text says.
Most importantly, keep walking until the whole counsel of Scripture leads your eyes to Christ.

And if grace has already pulled you out of something you thought would destroy you, tell your testimony. Somebody scrolling through those comments may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores people.
Do not keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty, but because somebody in your circle may be wrestling with this exact passage—or with the God they think this passage portrays.
Let them see that biblical faith does not require intellectual dishonesty.
Numbers 31 is not a chapter most people understand after one hurried reading.
There is another practical way you can help this ministry continue.
It cannot buy salvation, increase Christ's love for you, or make you more righteous before God.

But voluntary, cheerful financial support can function as a genuine offering toward ministry work—helping Gospel Warrior continue creating, researching, publishing, and expanding Christ-centered resources for people around the world.
If you believe this work glorifies God, one meaningful way to participate in it is to help sustain it.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Point somebody toward Jesus.
Those things matter too.
If you want to become part of that support:
Give freely.
Give prayerfully.
Never from manipulation or fear.
Support the Gospel because Christ is worthy, not because anyone promised you that a monthly payment could purchase His blessing.
And whatever you do after reading Numbers 31, do not walk away merely fascinated by ancient violence.
Walk away asking whether there is anything inside you that still needs to surrender.
Because the most dangerous battlefield may not be somewhere in Midian.
It may be the hidden territory of the human heart.
And the greatest wonder of Scripture is not that sinners can hide from judgment forever.
It is that sinners can run directly to Jesus and find mercy.
The sword in Numbers 31 should make us tremble—but the scars in the hands of Jesus should make us run home.
